title: From Software Developer to AI Engineer: Antje Barth

summary: Antje Barth outlines five practical steps for moving from software developer to AI engineer. Step one is understanding foundation model basics—why models produce unexpected output, how to customize via fine-tuning, and how to include function calling. She recommends the deeplearning.ai course 'Generative AI with Large Language Models.' Step two is getting hands-on with AI developer tools, noting up to 70% of developer time is spent on boilerplate, documentation, and legacy maintenance. AWS built Amazon Q Developer, a generative AI assistant that performs agentic tasks like feature development and code transformations (e.g., Java migrations). A demo by Mike Chambers shows Q Developer chatting in the IDE, explaining legacy code, generating functions, and using /dev to plan multi-file changes. Step three is prototyping and building with AI: defining use cases, choosing and customizing models (prompt engineering, RAG, fine-tuning), embedding responsible AI policies, guardrails, and managing GenOps/LLMOps. She stresses no one model rules them all, motivating Amazon Bedrock—a managed service offering leading models from multiple providers plus Amazon Titan. The unified Converse API standardizes parameters and output across models with native function calling. Step three also covers agents, demonstrated via a Minecraft-playing agent built in the Bedrock agents console using Claude 3 Haiku, with action groups for in-game actions (jump, dig, get player location, move to location). The agent reasons through multiple steps to solve problems—for example, when asked to 'come to me,' it identifies the requester, finds their location, and pathfinds to them, all in real time. Step five is staying up to date by engaging with community. Antje announces the transformation of the AWS Loft in San Francisco into an AI engineering hub for community workshops, events, and meetups, and invites attendees to suggest topics and apply to speak or host meetups.

takeaways: The AI engineer role reduces what took months or years to a few API calls, but understanding foundation model basics still matters.
Amazon Q Developer is an agentic assistant beyond code completion, capable of feature development and code transformations like Java upgrades.
Up to 70% of developer time is spent on non-creative tasks; generative AI tools aim to reclaim that for valuable work.
Amazon Bedrock provides a managed, secure way to access multiple leading foundation models—no single model fits all use cases.
The unified Converse API standardizes invocation parameters and output across different models with native function calling.
Agents built in the AWS Bedrock console can reason through multi-step problems; the Minecraft agent demo shows pathfinding and tool chaining in real time.
Staying up to date and engaging with community is essential in the fast-moving AI space.
AWS is transforming its San Francisco Loft into an AI engineering hub for community workshops, events, and meetups.

sections.title: Introduction and the AI Engineer Role
sections.summary: Antje introduces her talk on five practical steps from software developer to AI engineer, referencing swix's post defining the AI engineer role and noting that AI projects that took months or years can now be done with a few API calls, though understanding foundation model basics remains important.

sections.title: Step 1: Understand the Basics
sections.summary: Explains that AI engineers should understand foundation models, why they produce unexpected output, how to customize via fine-tuning, and how to include function calling. Recommends the deeplearning.ai course 'Generative AI with Large Language Models,' co-created with Andrew Ng's team and colleagues.

sections.title: Step 2: AI Developer Tools and Amazon Q Demo
sections.summary: Discusses English as a popular programming language for English-to-code and code-to-English tasks. Notes 70% of dev time is non-valuable work. Introduces Amazon Q Developer as an agentic assistant beyond code completion. Mike Chambers demos Q in an IDE: serverless app chat, code explanation, function generation, and /dev multi-file planning.

sections.title: Step 3: Prototyping and Building with AI
sections.summary: Covers the building workflow: use case definition, model choice, customization (prompt engineering, RAG, fine-tuning), responsible AI, guardrails, agents, and GenOps/LLMOps. Stresses no one model rules them all, motivating Amazon Bedrock as a managed service with leading models from multiple providers plus Amazon Titan, with secure data control.

sections.title: Unified Converse API
sections.summary: Introduces the new unified Converse API in Amazon Bedrock, standardizing parameters, prompts, and output across models with native function calling. Shows a Python example with message and tool lists. Claude 3.5 Sonnet was recently integrated. Points to community.aws resources by Dennis Trope.

sections.title: Agents Demo: Minecraft Agent
sections.summary: Mike Chambers walks through the Bedrock agents console showing a Minecraft-playing agent built with Claude 3 Haiku. Covers agent instructions as prompt engineering, action groups (Minecraft actions, experimental), and specific actions like jump, dig, get player location, and move to location, each linked to code with required parameters. Live demo shows the agent 'Rocky' in-game; when asked to 'come to me,' it reasons through identifying the requester, finding their location, and pathfinding to them in real time. Project code is available on GitHub.

sections.title: Step 5: Stay Up to Date and Community Announcement
sections.summary: Antje introduces the final step: staying up to date by engaging with community. She announces the transformation of the AWS Loft in San Francisco into an AI engineering hub for workshops, events, and meetups, inviting attendees to suggest topics via survey and apply to speak or host meetups. Mentions a happy hour with Anthropic that evening at The Loft and promises more events in upcoming weeks. Closes by recapping the five practical steps and encouraging attendees to innovate and visit the AWS booth.

demonstrations: Mike Chambers demos Amazon Q Developer inside an IDE: chatting to create a serverless app, explaining legacy code, generating a string-trimming function, and using /dev to plan and insert a multi-file DynamoDB search-by-category feature.
Python code example showing the unified Converse API: defining message lists, system/user prompts, inference parameters, model ID selection (Anthropic), and a tool list for function calling.

Minecraft-playing agent demo: configured with Claude 3 Haiku in Bedrock agents console, with action groups for jump, dig, get player location, and move to location. The agent 'Rocky' reasons through multi-step actions in-game—identifying the requester, finding their location, and pathfinding to them when asked to 'come to me.'
